title: Data Transfer Costs
summary: Where AWS charges for moving bytes, and the designs that avoid those charges.
tldr: Rule of thumb: data **into** AWS is free; data **out** to the internet, **between Regions** and **between AZs** costs money; traffic inside one AZ over private IPs is free.
Cut internet egress with **CloudFront** (origin-to-CloudFront transfer from AWS origins is free and edge rates are lower) or **Direct Connect** for steady on-premises downloads.

Cut cross-AZ and inter-Region charges by keeping chatty components together: same-AZ routing, cluster placement groups for disposable clusters, and a **local replica** of data read repeatedly from another Region.
Large VPC-to-VPC flows through a Transit Gateway pay per-GB processing; a **VPC peering** connection for that pair avoids it.

keyFacts.text: Traffic between instances in the same AZ over private IPs is free, including over VPC peering. Crossing AZs is billed in **both** directions.
AZ names (us-east-1a) map to different physical zones per account. Use AZ IDs (use1-az1) to co-locate resources across accounts.
CloudFront price classes exclude the most expensive edge locations. Viewers elsewhere are still served, just from a farther edge.
Data transfer out over Direct Connect is billed at a lower per-GB rate than over the internet or a Site-to-Site VPN.
The CUR usage type for cross-AZ traffic in a Region. A big line here points to chatty services spread across AZs.

keywords.answer: Match AZ IDs, not AZ names

traps: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads over long distances but **adds** cost; it never reduces egress charges.
Using public IPs or an internet gateway between instances doesn't avoid cross-AZ charges and adds public IPv4 cost.
Global Accelerator improves performance and failover; it isn't a cheaper path for bulk data.
Geo-restriction blocks users; it is wrong when the question says the remaining viewers must still be served.
Matching AZ *names* across accounts doesn't guarantee the same physical AZ.
